events.title: Siege of Hippo Regius and death of Augustine
events.summary: From about June 430 Gaiseric besieged Bonifatius in Hippo Regius for fourteen months. In the third month, on 28 August 430, the city's bishop Augustine died aged 75, reading the penitential psalms fixed to his wall. The Vandals lifted the siege in summer 431 and the inhabitants then abandoned the city; Augustine's library survived.

sides.strength: Bonifatius's Gothic federates and local levies

sides.losses: heavy from hunger, according to Procopius

battle.significance: The Vandals lacked siege skills; an eastern army under Aspar arrived in 431 but was defeated with Bonifatius in 432, leaving Africa open.

events.title: First Council of Ephesus
events.summary: Summoned by Theodosius II, the council opened on 22 June 431 under Cyril of Alexandria before John of Antioch and the eastern bishops arrived, and deposed Nestorius of Constantinople for refusing Mary the title Theotokos (God-bearer). John's rival council deposed Cyril. The emperor at first confirmed both depositions, then sided with Cyril.
events.detail: Cyril spent lavishly on bribes (eulogiae) at court, an inventory of which survives. The Formula of Reunion of 433 reconciled Cyril and John, but Nestorius was exiled to the Great Oasis of Egypt. The Church of the East in Persia later adopted a dyophysite theology labelled 'Nestorian' by its enemies, carrying Syriac Christianity to Central Asia and China.
events.debate: The role of Pulcheria, whom Nestorius had offended, is emphasised by Holum and doubted by others. Whether Nestorius actually held the 'two sons' heresy he was condemned for is a long-running question.
scholarship: McGuckin, St Cyril of Alexandria: The Christological Controversy (1994)
Holum, Theodosian Empresses (1982)

events.title: Battle of Rimini: Aetius against Bonifatius
events.summary: Placidia recalled Bonifatius from Africa, made him patricius and magister militum and dismissed Aetius. Aetius marched on Italy; near Ariminum Bonifatius won but was mortally wounded and died months later. Aetius fled to the Huns and returned in 433 with Hunnic backing, forcing Placidia to accept him as patricius in 435.

battle.significance: A pyrrhic victory for the court: it removed Aetius's main rival and opened two decades of Aetius's ascendancy, built on Hunnic support.

events.debate: Later tradition says Aetius had a longer spear prepared for a duel with Bonifatius; this is likely legend.

events.title: Treaty of Margus with the Huns
events.summary: After the death of Rua, his nephews Bleda and Attila met eastern envoys on horseback outside Margus on the Danube. Constantinople agreed to double the annual payment to 700 lbs of gold, return Hunnic fugitives, pay 8 solidi for each escaped Roman prisoner and open markets on equal terms.
events.debate: Date is 435 or 439; Priscus survives only in Constantinian excerpts.

events.title: Treaty of Hippo with the Vandals
events.summary: On 11 February 435 Ravenna recognised the Vandals as federates in Mauretania Sitifensis and parts of Numidia, in return for tribute and Gaiseric's son Huneric as hostage, keeping Carthage and the rich Proconsular province for Rome.

events.title: Huns destroy the Burgundian kingdom on the Rhine
events.summary: After the Burgundians under King Gundahar pushed into Belgica, Aetius defeated them in 435 and then set Hunnic auxiliaries on them in 436/437: Gundahar was killed with, according to Hydatius, 20,000 of his people. The survivors were resettled in Sapaudia (Savoy) in 443. The catastrophe became the core of the Nibelungenlied.

battle.significance: Demonstrated Aetius's method of using Huns to discipline federates, and fixed the Burgundians in the Rhône valley, where they founded their second kingdom.

events.debate: The Worms location is from the medieval epic; the kingdom's centre in the 430s is uncertain (perhaps the middle Rhine or Main valley).

events.title: Publication of the Theodosian Code
events.summary: Promulgated by Theodosius II on 15 February 438 and in force from 1 January 439 in both halves of the empire, the Codex Theodosianus collected about 2,500 general constitutions issued since Constantine in 312, arranged in 16 books by subject and date. On 25 December 438 the Roman Senate received it with recorded acclamations, chanted 28 times or more.
events.detail: The commission of 429 had planned a second, comprehensive code combining juristic writings, which was never realised; Justinian achieved that a century later. The Code is our richest source for late Roman government: book 16 on religion, books on the cursus publicus, curiales, coloni and military matters. It survives incompletely: books 1-5 depend on the Breviary of Alaric (506). The Gesta Senatus of 438 preserve the acclamations and the procedure of reception, with orders to make official copies.

sources.w: Gesta senatus Romani de Theodosiano publicando

scholarship: Matthews, Laying Down the Law: A Study of the Theodosian Code (2000)
Harries & Wood (eds.), The Theodosian Code (1993)
Honoré, Law in the Crisis of Empire 379-455 AD (1998)

events.title: Battle of Toulouse: capture of Litorius
events.summary: Litorius, Aetius's deputy, who had relieved the Gothic siege of Narbonne in 437, attacked Theodoric I's capital Toulouse with Hunnic auxiliaries. Salvian and Prosper say he consulted pagan auspices. He was defeated, captured and executed; Avitus then negotiated peace with the Goths.

sides.strength: Roman troops and Hunnic auxiliaries under Litorius

battle.significance: Ended Roman attempts to reduce the Visigoths by force; thereafter they were managed by treaty.

events.title: Gaiseric seizes Carthage
events.summary: Breaking the 435 treaty, Gaiseric took Carthage by surprise on 19 October 439. The second city of the West, its fleet, and the Proconsular province, the West's richest tax base and Rome's granary, passed to the Vandals. The Vandal kingdom dated its years from this day.
events.detail: The loss of Africa Proconsularis and Byzacena deprived the western government of perhaps a third or more of its revenue and much of Rome's grain. Gaiseric expropriated the senatorial and church estates of the Proconsularis (the sortes Vandalorum), exiled Nicene bishops, and turned Carthage's shipyards to piracy: Sicily was raided in 440. Heather treats 439 as the decisive blow to western fiscal viability.

sides.strength: city garrison; no field army in Africa

battle.significance: The most damaging single loss the western empire suffered: revenue, grain and a naval base turned against Italy.

scholarship: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Merrills & Miles, The Vandals (2010)

events.title: Aborted East-West expedition against the Vandals
events.summary: Theodosius II assembled a fleet of about 1,100 transports under five generals in Sicily in 441 to retake Carthage, but recalled it when the Persians attacked in Armenia and the Huns crossed the Danube. The 442 treaty left the Vandals the Proconsularis, Byzacena and Tripolitania and engaged Huneric to Valentinian's daughter Eudocia.
events.debate: Heather suggests the Huns deliberately attacked to wreck the expedition, perhaps in concert with Gaiseric; there is no direct evidence of collusion.

events.title: Huns sack Naissus
events.summary: In 441-442 the Huns of Bleda and Attila took Viminacium, Margus (betrayed by its bishop), Singidunum and Sirmium, then besieged Naissus, Constantine's birthplace, with rams and siege towers (Priscus describes their wheeled beams). The city fell; years later Priscus found the riverbank still strewn with bones.

battle.significance: Showed that the Huns, unlike earlier steppe raiders, could take fortified cities with captured Roman engineering skills.

events.debate: Date 442 or 443.

events.title: Peace of Anatolius with the Huns
events.summary: After defeats in Thrace, Constantinople agreed to pay 6,000 lbs of gold in arrears and to triple the annual tribute to 2,100 lbs, and to ransom Roman prisoners at 12 solidi each. Priscus describes senators selling their wives' jewellery and furniture to raise the sums.
events.debate: 2,100 lbs a year was perhaps 2-3% of eastern revenue; Priscus's complaint reflects the burden on the senatorial class rather than imperial insolvency.

events.title: Earthquake and rebuilding of the Theodosian Walls
events.summary: An earthquake on 26 January 447 threw down much of the land wall, including 57 towers, as Attila advanced. The praetorian prefect Constantinus mobilised the Blue and Green circus factions and rebuilt it in about two months, adding the outer wall and moat. Inscriptions at the Mevlevihane Gate boast that 'not even Pallas could have built so quickly'.

events.title: Battle of the Utus
events.summary: In 447 Attila's army met the eastern field army under the magister Arnegisclus on the river Utus (Vit) in Dacia Ripensis. Arnegisclus was killed fighting after his horse fell; the Huns won but at heavy cost, then sacked Marcianople and raided as far as Thermopylae and the Gallipoli peninsula.

battle.significance: The last pitched battle of the eastern army against Attila; afterwards Theodosius accepted humiliating terms, including a demilitarised strip south of the Danube five days' journey wide.

events.title: Embassy of Maximinus and Priscus to Attila
events.summary: Priscus of Panium accompanied the envoy Maximinus to Attila's wooden capital north of the Danube, unaware that the eunuch Chrysaphius had bribed Attila's officer Edeco to murder the king. Edeco betrayed the plot. Priscus's account is the only eyewitness description of the Hunnic court: Attila's simple wooden cup amid gold plate, the stone bath built by a captured Roman engineer, and a Greek merchant turned Hun who praised life outside Roman taxes and lawyers.
events.detail: The Greek ex-merchant's debate with Priscus, in which he argues that Roman law is just in theory but corrupt and ruinous in practice, is a famous set piece, probably shaped by Priscus as a literary dialogue. The embassy met envoys from the West, among them Orestes's colleague Romulus (grandfather of Romulus Augustulus) and Orestes himself served Attila as secretary. Onegesius, Attila's chief minister, and Berichus feature as well.
events.debate: Priscus survives only in Constantine VII's Excerpta de legationibus and in Jordanes's paraphrase; the location of Attila's court (somewhere on the Tisza plain) is unknown.
scholarship: Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians of the Later Roman Empire (1981-83)
Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
Kelly, Attila the Hun: Barbarian Terror and the Fall of the Roman Empire (2008)

events.title: Second Council of Ephesus (the 'Robber Synod')
events.summary: Presided over by Dioscorus of Alexandria with imperial backing, the August 449 council rehabilitated the monk Eutyches, refused to read Pope Leo's Tome, and deposed Flavian of Constantinople, who died after rough handling. Leo called it a latrocinium, a gang of robbers.

events.title: Death of Theodosius II; Marcian chosen
events.summary: Theodosius II died on 28 July 450 after a fall from his horse while hunting. His sister Pulcheria, a consecrated virgin, married the retired officer Marcian (with a vow of chastity respected) and he was crowned on 25 August. Chrysaphius was executed and the tribute to Attila stopped.
events.debate: Aspar, Marcian's patron, was the real kingmaker. Marcian's halt to tribute redirected Attila westward.

events.title: Honoria's appeal to Attila
events.summary: Justa Grata Honoria, Valentinian III's sister, disgraced after an affair with her steward Eugenius and betrothed against her will to the senator Herculanus, sent her eunuch Hyacinthus with a ring to Attila asking for help. Attila claimed her as his bride with half the western empire as dowry, a pretext for invading Gaul.
events.debate: Some scholars doubt the story entirely as court gossip; Jordanes dates the affair to 434 and has Honoria pregnant and sent to Constantinople.

events.title: Huns sack Metz
events.summary: Crossing the Rhine in spring 451, Attila's army stormed Divodurum (Metz) on the eve of Easter, 7 April, burning the city and killing the priest at the altar; only the oratory of St Stephen survived, according to Gregory of Tours.

battle.significance: Opened Attila's march into the heart of Gaul.

events.title: Siege of Orléans
events.summary: Attila besieged Aurelianum, where an Alan group was settled; Bishop Anianus organised the defence. The Huns had breached the walls when Aetius and Theodoric I arrived around mid-June and forced them to withdraw eastward toward the Catalaunian Plains.

sides.strength: citizens and Alan settlers, relieved by Aetius's coalition

battle.significance: The turning point of the 451 campaign: the relief of Orléans denied Attila the Loire and the Visigothic south.

events.title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.summary: Aetius, with Visigoths under Theodoric I, Alans under Sangiban, Franks, Burgundians and others, fought Attila's Huns, Ostrogoths and Gepids on the Campus Mauriacus or Catalaunian Plains in Champagne. Theodoric was killed, but Attila was driven into his wagon laager, reportedly ready to burn himself on a pyre of saddles. Aetius let him withdraw.
events.detail: Jordanes, our main source, gives 165,000 dead, an impossible figure. His account comes through Cassiodorus and perhaps Priscus, and is shaped to glorify Goths on both sides: the Visigoths win the day, and Ostrogoths fight unwillingly for Attila. The tactical narrative involves a struggle for a ridge, Sangiban's Alans placed in the centre because their loyalty was doubted, and Thorismund, Theodoric's son, sent home by Aetius, who wanted neither Huns nor Goths too strong. Often hailed as a battle that saved Western civilisation, it was in fact a hard-fought draw: Attila invaded Italy the next year.

sides.strength: unknown; perhaps 30,000-50,000 including Visigoths, Alans, Franks, Burgundians, Saxons, Armoricans
unknown; Huns with Ostrogoths under Valamir, Gepids under Ardaric and others

battle.significance: Halted Attila in Gaul and preserved Aetius's coalition, but did not destroy Hunnic power. It was the last great campaign of a western Roman field army in Gaul.

events.debate: Site disputed: near Châlons-en-Champagne, near Troyes (Campus Mauriacus, possibly Méry-sur-Seine), or elsewhere. The 20 June date is a modern reconstruction; some argue for September. Jordanes's Getica is a Gothic-centred compression of Cassiodorus written c. 551 in Constantinople and its numbers are worthless.
scholarship: Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Kim, The Huns (2016)
Hughes, Patricius: The Life and Times of Flavius Aetius (2012)

events.title: Battle of Avarayr
events.summary: Armenian nobles under Vardan Mamikonian, rebelling against Yazdegerd II's attempt to impose Zoroastrianism, were crushed on the plain of Avarayr. Vardan and eight other commanders were killed; Marcian refused to help. The resistance continued as guerrilla war and won religious freedom in the Treaty of Nvarsak (484).

battle.significance: A defeat remembered as a national-religious victory; it also demonstrated Constantinople's refusal to break the peace with Persia while Attila threatened.

sources.w: History of Vardan and the Armenian War

events.debate: Armenian sources are hagiographic; numbers unreliable. The date (26 May or 2 June 451) depends on the Armenian church calendar.

events.title: Council of Chalcedon
events.summary: Convened by Marcian and Pulcheria at Chalcedon, across the Bosporus from Constantinople, from 8 October to 1 November 451, with some 520 bishops (tradition says 630). It deposed Dioscorus, accepted Leo's Tome and defined Christ as one person 'in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'.
events.detail: The definition split eastern Christianity permanently. Egypt and much of Syria rejected it as Nestorianism revived; the miaphysite (anti-Chalcedonian) churches, later Coptic, Syriac Orthodox and Armenian, grew from this rejection, and imperial attempts to bridge the gap (Henotikon 482, Justinian's Three Chapters 553, Heraclius's Monoenergism and Monotheletism 633-638) all failed. Canon 28 granted Constantinople privileges equal to Old Rome as 'New Rome'; Leo refused to accept it. Older scholarship blamed the schism for weakening loyalty to Constantinople in Egypt and Syria before the Arab conquests; this is now generally rejected or heavily qualified.
scholarship: Price & Gaddis, The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (2005)
Gray, The Defense of Chalcedon in the East 451-553 (1979)
Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972)

events.title: Attila destroys Aquileia
events.summary: In spring 452 Attila crossed the Julian Alps and besieged Aquileia for some three months; Procopius and Jordanes tell that he was about to give up when he saw storks carrying their young out of the city and took it as an omen. The city was stormed and destroyed so thoroughly that it never fully recovered.

battle.significance: Aquileia's fall opened the Po valley; refugees fleeing to the lagoons figure in the foundation legends of Venice and Grado.

events.title: Pope Leo meets Attila on the Mincio
events.summary: After sacking Patavium, Vicetia, Verona, Brixia, Bergamum, Mediolanum and Ticinum, Attila received an embassy of Pope Leo I, the ex-consul Gennadius Avienus and the ex-prefect Trygetius at the ager Ambuleius on the Mincio near Mantua. He withdrew from Italy soon after.
events.detail: Prosper, Leo's secretary, credits the pope; Hydatius instead credits famine, disease and an eastern army under Marcian's general Aetius (not the patrician) crossing the Danube to strike the Hunnic homeland. Later legend added Saints Peter and Paul threatening Attila with swords, painted by Raphael in the Vatican.
events.locName: Ager Ambuleius on the Mincio, near Mantua
events.debate: Classic case of competing explanations: papal prestige (Prosper), logistics and disease (Hydatius), and Attila's fear of Alaric's fate after taking Rome (Jordanes).

events.title: Death of Attila
events.summary: Attila died in early 453 on the night of his wedding to a girl named Ildico, choking on a haemorrhage from the nose while drunk, according to Priscus via Jordanes. His men cut their faces so that the greatest of warriors would be mourned with blood, not tears, and buried him secretly in coffins of gold, silver and iron.
events.debate: Marcellinus Comes records a rumour that Ildico stabbed him; the strava funeral chant in Jordanes is often taken as authentic Priscan material.

events.title: Battle of the Nedao
events.summary: Attila's sons quarrelled over the subject peoples 'as if they were household slaves' (Jordanes). Ardaric of the Gepids led a revolt and defeated the Huns on the unidentified river Nedao in Pannonia; Attila's eldest son Ellac was killed with 30,000 of his followers. The Hunnic empire disintegrated.

sides.strength: Gepids under Ardaric with Rugii, Suebi, Heruli and others

battle.significance: Freed the Danubian peoples (Gepids, Ostrogoths, Rugii, Heruli, Sciri) who would dominate the next generation of Balkan and Italian politics.

events.debate: Date 454 or 455; location unknown. Whether the Ostrogoths fought with or against the Huns is unclear from Jordanes.

events.title: Valentinian III murders Aetius
events.summary: During a financial report at the palace in Rome on 21 (or 22) September 454, Valentinian III, aged 35 and at last asserting himself, attacked Aetius with his own sword, and the chamberlain Heraclius finished him. A courtier is supposed to have told the emperor he had cut off his right hand with his left.
events.debate: The trigger was Aetius's push to marry his son Gaudentius to Valentinian's daughter Placidia. Petronius Maximus and Heraclius are said to have stoked the emperor's fear.

events.title: Assassination of Valentinian III
events.summary: On 16 March 455, while Valentinian watched athletic exercises on the Campus Martius, two of Aetius's former bucellarii, Optila and Thraustila, cut him down along with Heraclius. The Theodosian dynasty in the West ended. The senator Petronius Maximus, probably the instigator, took the throne the next day and forced Valentinian's widow Licinia Eudoxia to marry him.

events.title: Vandal sack of Rome
events.summary: Claiming that the 442 betrothal of Huneric to Eudocia had been broken, Gaiseric landed at Portus. Petronius Maximus, fleeing, was stoned or torn apart by the crowd on 31 May 455. The Vandals entered on 2 June and, after Pope Leo secured a promise to avoid burning and massacre, systematically plundered the city for fourteen days.
events.detail: They took the empress Licinia Eudoxia and her daughters Eudocia and Placidia, thousands of captives, the treasures of the imperial palace, half the gilded bronze roof tiles of the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, and the spoils of the Jerusalem Temple brought by Titus in 70, which Belisarius would bring to Constantinople in 534. Eudocia married Huneric. The word 'vandalism' was coined in 1794 by Abbé Grégoire; ancient accounts suggest a methodical, not wanton, plundering.

sides.losses: emperor killed by mob; city plundered

sides.strength: Vandal and Moorish fleet and army

battle.significance: A far more thorough plundering than 410. It removed the last members of the Theodosian house from Italy and began twenty years of Vandal naval terror in the western Mediterranean.

events.debate: Procopius's claim that Eudoxia invited Gaiseric to avenge her husband is likely gossip. The Temple spoils' later fate is legendary.

events.title: Avitus proclaimed emperor with Visigothic support
events.summary: Eparchius Avitus, a Gallic aristocrat sent as envoy to the Visigothic king Theodoric II at Toulouse, was proclaimed emperor at Ugernum near Arles on 9 July 455 with Gothic backing and acclaimed by Gallic notables. His son-in-law Sidonius Apollinaris delivered his panegyric in Rome on 1 January 456.

events.title: Battle of the Órbigo: Visigoths crush the Suebi
events.summary: Acting nominally for Avitus, Theodoric II invaded Gallaecia and destroyed the army of the Suebic king Rechiar on the river Órbigo, twelve miles from Asturica (Astorga). Rechiar was captured and executed in December; the Suebic kingdom split into factions for a generation.
events.locName: Campus Paramus on the Órbigo, near Astorga

sides.strength: Visigothic army with Burgundian contingents under Theodoric II

sides.losses: heavy; king captured and later executed

battle.significance: Started the Visigothic shift into Spain that would eventually make it the heart of their kingdom.

events.title: Ricimer defeats the Vandals at Agrigentum and Corsica
events.summary: Ricimer, a general of Suevic and Visigothic royal descent, defeated a Vandal force near Agrigentum in Sicily and then a Vandal fleet of 60 ships off Corsica in 456. The prestige made him the decisive figure in Italy.

battle.significance: Launched Ricimer's sixteen-year dominance as king-maker of the West.

events.title: Battle of Placentia: fall of Avitus
events.summary: Ricimer and Majorian turned on Avitus, whose Visigothic allies were away in Spain. He was defeated at Placentia on 17 October 456, his general Messianus killed. Avitus was spared and consecrated bishop of Placentia, but died within months.

battle.significance: Ended the Gallo-Gothic experiment of an emperor from Gaul and established that Italy's army, under Ricimer, made emperors.

events.title: Accession of Leo I
events.summary: After Marcian's death on 27 January 457, Aspar, who as an Arian Alan could not take the throne himself, chose Leo, a tribune from Dacia. Leo was crowned on 7 February 457, possibly by the patriarch Anatolius, and later began building an Isaurian counterweight to Aspar's Goths.
events.debate: Whether Leo's was the first patriarchal coronation is disputed; De Ceremoniis describes a military raising on the shield with the patriarch present.

events.title: Majorian becomes emperor
events.summary: After months without an emperor in the West, Majorian, Aetius's former officer and Ricimer's comrade, was acclaimed by the army on 1 April 457 at Ad Columellas near Ravenna and became Augustus on 28 December 457. He was the last western emperor to campaign in person with real energy.

events.title: Majorian's legislation
events.summary: Majorian's Novels attacked tax arrears and abuses by collectors, restored the office of defensor civitatis, protected curiales, and in Novel 4 (11 July 458) forbade the stripping of ancient public buildings in Rome for building stone, with fines of 50 lbs of gold for officials who allowed it.

events.title: Majorian defeats Vandal raiders in Campania
events.summary: A Vandal and Moorish raiding force led by Gaiseric's brother-in-law landed at the mouth of the Liris (Garigliano) near Sinuessa and plundered Campania. Majorian's troops caught them laden with booty and drove them back to their ships with heavy losses; the Vandal leader was killed.

battle.significance: A morale boost that encouraged Majorian's plan to strike Carthage directly.

events.title: Vandals burn Majorian's fleet in Spain
events.summary: Majorian, having forced the Visigoths and Burgundians back into alliance, assembled a fleet of about 300 ships in the Spanish harbour of Portus Illicitanus (near Elche) and around Carthago Nova to invade Africa. Traitors guided Vandal raiders who burned or seized much of it in 460. Majorian made peace and returned to Italy.

sides.losses: most of the fleet destroyed or captured

battle.significance: The failure destroyed Majorian's prestige and led directly to his deposition.

events.debate: Procopius's tale that Majorian dyed his hair and visited Carthage in disguise as his own envoy is folklore.

events.title: Ricimer deposes and executes Majorian
events.summary: Returning to Italy after dismissing his army, Majorian was arrested by Ricimer at Dertona on 2 August 461, stripped of his purple, beaten and beheaded on 7 August near the river Iria. Procopius praises him as a ruler surpassing all who had gone before.

events.title: Aegidius defeats the Visigoths at Orléans
events.summary: Aegidius, magister militum per Gallias, refused to recognise Ricimer's puppet Libius Severus and fought the Visigoths, to whom Ricimer had ceded Narbonne. With Frankish help (Childeric?) he defeated a Gothic army near Orléans, killing Frederic, brother of Theodoric II. He died in 464 or 465, perhaps poisoned, leaving a Roman enclave around Soissons to his son Syagrius.

sides.strength: Gallic field army remnant with Frankish allies

battle.significance: Kept northern Gaul out of Visigothic hands, leaving it to be fought over by Romans and Franks.

events.title: Anthemius sent from Constantinople as western emperor
events.summary: After the death of Libius Severus in 465 and nearly two years without an emperor, Leo I sent the eastern aristocrat Anthemius, son-in-law of Marcian, with an army and Marcellinus of Dalmatia. He was proclaimed near Rome on 12 April 467; his daughter Alypia married Ricimer to seal the arrangement.

events.title: Battle of Cape Bon: the great Vandal expedition fails
events.summary: The largest naval expedition of late antiquity, sent by Leo I under his brother-in-law Basiliscus, anchored off Cape Bon (Promunturium Mercurii) some 60 km from Carthage. Gaiseric bought a five-day truce, then sent fireships among the crowded fleet with a favourable wind. Half the fleet was lost; Basiliscus fled.
events.detail: The cost was staggering: John Lydus reports 65,000 lbs of gold and 700,000 lbs of silver; Procopius 130,000 lbs of gold. Later Byzantine sources speak of 1,113 ships and 100,000 men. It nearly bankrupted the eastern treasury for a generation, and its failure ended any realistic hope of restoring the West's African tax base. Simultaneous operations had gone well: Marcellinus cleared Sardinia and Heraclius of Edessa took Tripolitania. Procopius reports the heroism of the general John, who leapt armoured into the sea rather than surrender to Gaiseric's son Genzo. Suspicion that Basiliscus was bribed, or acting for Aspar, who wanted the expedition to fail, appears in the sources.

battle.significance: The decisive failure of the late Roman effort to recover Africa; it sealed the western empire's fiscal fate and crippled eastern finances until Anastasius.

events.debate: Figures for ships and cost differ widely; Heather accepts the scale as broadly real. Blame on Basiliscus and Aspar may be propaganda from Zeno's later regime.

events.title: Battle of Déols: Riothamus defeated
events.summary: Anthemius's ally Riothamus, 'king of the Britons', crossed with an army Jordanes puts at 12,000 to Berry to fight Euric, but was defeated near Bourg-de-Déols before Roman forces could join him and fled to the Burgundians. Euric then took much of central Gaul.

battle.significance: Removed the last field army able to contest Euric's expansion north of the Loire.

events.debate: Whether Riothamus's Britons came from Britain or from Armorica is debated; his identification with a historical Arthur (Ashe) has little support.

events.title: Leo I murders Aspar
events.summary: After fifty years as Constantinople's kingmaker, the Alan general Aspar and his son Ardabur were cut down by palace eunuchs in 471 on Leo's orders; Leo earned the nickname Makelles, 'the Butcher'. The Isaurian Zeno, married to Leo's daughter Ariadne since 466/467, inherited Aspar's role. Aspar's Gothic followers rose under Theodoric Strabo.

events.title: Sieges of Clermont
events.summary: For four summers the Arverni, led by Bishop Sidonius Apollinaris and his brother-in-law Ecdicius (who once broke through the Gothic lines with eighteen horsemen), resisted Euric's Goths. In 475 Julius Nepos ceded Auvergne in exchange for Provence; Sidonius, who felt betrayed, was briefly imprisoned.

sides.strength: citizens and private retainers of Ecdicius

battle.significance: The Auvergne's sacrifice in the 475 treaty marked Ravenna's abandonment of Roman Gaul north of the Durance.

events.title: Ricimer besieges Rome; death of Anthemius
events.summary: Ricimer quarrelled with his father-in-law Anthemius and besieged him in Rome in spring 472, proclaiming Olybrius emperor in April. After famine and street fighting the city fell; Anthemius, hiding disguised as a beggar in St Peter's or Santa Maria in Trastevere, was beheaded by Ricimer's nephew Gundobad on 11 July 472.

sides.strength: Anthemius's guards, citizens and Gothic troops under Bilimer from Gaul

battle.significance: The first time Rome was stormed by a Roman army since 312, and the end of the last East-backed attempt to stabilise the West.

events.title: Death of Ricimer
events.summary: Ricimer died on 18 August 472, vomiting blood, five weeks after killing Anthemius. Olybrius died on 2 November. Gundobad inherited the post of patricius and in March 473 made the comes domesticorum Glycerius emperor before leaving to claim the Burgundian throne.
scholarship: MacGeorge, Late Roman Warlords (2002)
Anders, Flavius Ricimer (2010)

events.title: Zeno becomes emperor
events.summary: Leo I died on 18 January 474, leaving his seven-year-old grandson Leo II, son of Zeno and Ariadne. Leo II crowned his father Zeno co-emperor on 9 February and died in November 474, leaving the Isaurian, born Tarasis son of Kodisa, sole Augustus.

events.title: Julius Nepos deposes Glycerius
events.summary: Leo I refused to recognise Glycerius and sent Julius Nepos, magister militum of Dalmatia and nephew of Marcellinus, who landed at Portus in June 474. Glycerius surrendered without a fight and was consecrated bishop of Salona.

events.title: Zeno's 'endless peace' with Gaiseric
events.summary: Zeno's envoy, the senator Severus, negotiated a perpetual peace: Constantinople recognised Vandal rule in Africa, Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and the Balearics, and Gaiseric released captives and allowed Nicene worship in Carthage. It held until 533.

events.title: Usurpation of Basiliscus
events.summary: In January 475 Leo's widow Verina and her brother Basiliscus drove Zeno back to Isauria. Basiliscus issued an Encyclical condemning Chalcedon, sparking riots led by Daniel the Stylite, then withdrew it. Illus and Verina's associates switched sides, and Zeno re-entered Constantinople in August 476. Basiliscus and his family were starved to death in a cistern at Limnae in Cappadocia.
events.detail: A great fire in 475 destroyed the Basilica library (said to have held 120,000 books, including a 120-foot dragon-gut copy of Homer) and the Lauseion palace with its famous collection of Greek statues.

events.title: Orestes drives out Nepos; Romulus Augustulus proclaimed
events.summary: Orestes, a Pannonian Roman who had been Attila's secretary and was now Nepos's magister militum, turned the army on his master. Nepos fled from Ravenna to Dalmatia on 28 August 475, and on 31 October Orestes proclaimed his own adolescent son Romulus emperor, mocked as Augustulus.

events.title: Odoacer kills Orestes at Placentia
events.summary: The barbarian federates of the Italian army, Heruli, Sciri, Rugii and Turcilingi, demanded a third of the land of Italy. Orestes refused. They proclaimed the Scirian officer Odoacer king on 23 August 476, besieged Orestes in Ticinum, and captured and executed him at Placentia on 28 August; his brother Paulus was killed in the pine forest outside Ravenna on 4 September.

sides.strength: federate troops of the Italian army

battle.significance: Destroyed the last Roman regime in Italy and transferred power to the federate army that had long been its real base.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.summary: Odoacer entered Ravenna, deposed the boy emperor Romulus but spared him 'because of his beauty', gave him a pension of 6,000 solidi and sent him to live with his relatives at the Castellum Lucullanum near Naples. Odoacer ruled Italy as king, nominally under Constantinople, and did not appoint another western emperor.
events.detail: The Senate sent the imperial regalia to Zeno with a message that one emperor sufficed for both halves and asking that Odoacer be made patricius. Zeno replied that they had a legitimate emperor, Nepos, and should take him back; he addressed Odoacer as patricius anyway. Nepos lived in Dalmatia until 480 and was recognised on Odoacer's coins. Contemporaries barely noticed 476; the idea that the western empire 'fell' then was constructed in the 510s-520s at Constantinople, notably by Marcellinus Comes ('the Hesperian empire of the Roman people perished with this Augustulus'), as Croke showed. Romulus may still have been alive in 507-511, when Cassiodorus's Variae mentions a Romulus receiving a pension.
events.debate: The core of the 'fall vs transformation' debate. Ward-Perkins and Heather insist on a real political collapse with severe material consequences; Goffart, Halsall and the 'Transformation of the Roman World' project stress continuity of Roman administration, law and elites under barbarian kings. Kaldellis argues that from Constantinople's viewpoint the empire continued and merely lost western provinces.
scholarship: Croke, 'AD 476: the manufacture of a turning point', Chiron 13 (1983)
Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)
Goffart, Barbarian Tides (2006)
Kaldellis, The New Roman Empire (2023)
